title: Mysterious object in the sky of Ohio, pilots photograph an unusual body that did not appear on radar
excerpt: Mysterious object in the sky of Ohio, pilots photograph an unusual body that did not appear on radar
content:
mystery

Express newspaper

31/10/2026 18:03

An unidentified flying object, shaped like a capsule and with a reflective metallic surface, has been reported by pilots of a plane flying over the US state of Ohio. According to their testimony, the object was observed at an altitude of about 13 kilometers, but did not appear on air traffic control radar systems. The case has raised questions about flight safety and the identification of unknown objects in airspace.

The event occurred on August 16, while the report about it was published on October 26 by the National UFO Reporting Center (NUFORC), an American organization that collects and examines evidence of unidentified objects.

According to the report, the pilots were flying over Ohio when they noticed an unusual object, silver in color and elongated in shape, that appeared almost motionless as the plane approached.

One of the pilots, identified only by the initial "J", managed to photograph the object with his phone.

"It looked like polished metal, without any marks or deformation"

The pilot described the object during an interview with NUFORC investigator Ben Hansen.

"The surface was silvery and highly reflective, like pure, polished metal," the investigator's report states.

According to the testimony, the object had a uniform shape, similar to a capsule or pill, without wrinkles, deformations or constrictions at the top and bottom.

The pilot estimated that the object could have been at least nine meters high.

He initially suspected it might be a weather balloon, but the regular shape and atmospheric conditions made him question this explanation.

The object was spotted near the clouds of a powerful storm

At around 20:00 p.m. local time in the eastern United States, the plane was flying at an altitude of 41 feet, approximately 12.500 meters.

At that moment, the pilots were approaching a powerful storm, whose clouds reached up to 55 thousand feet, or about 16.800 meters.

To avoid the most dangerous parts of the storm, the crew decided to pass through a gap between the clouds.

It was then that the pilot noticed the mysterious object, just above the plane.

Initially, he thought the object was about eight kilometers away, but later revised the estimate to approximately three to five kilometers.

According to the pilots, the object was at an altitude of about 43 feet, approximately 13.100 meters, and appeared to be moving in the opposite direction to the plane, passing on its left side.

The pilot believed that the object's glow came from the reflection of sunlight and not from any internal source of illumination.

No trace on air traffic control radars

The encounter with the object lasted approximately two minutes.

According to flight data later submitted by the pilot, the plane was traveling at a speed of about 610 kilometers per hour.

About a minute after spotting the object, the pilot contacted air traffic controllers at Cleveland Center to ask if there were any other aircraft or weather balloons in the area.

Neither the plane's collision warning system nor the flight tracking app showed any other aircraft.

According to the pilot's testimony, air traffic controllers also confirmed that they were not seeing any objects on their radars.

The crew continued to observe the object until it disappeared into the distance, behind the aircraft.

The pilot was only able to take a picture of it with his iPhone after the object had passed them. At that moment, he estimated it was about 11 kilometers away from the plane.

He emphasized that the detailed description of the object's shape and surface was based on observation made when the object was much closer.

Could it have been a weather balloon?

One of the possible explanations considered by investigators was the presence of a weather balloon.

However, according to the NUFORC report, no data was found consistent with planned balloon releases in that area.

The organization also reported that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had not identified the object on radar.

Investigator Ben Hansen emphasized that the dimensions estimated by the witness and the uniform shape of the object created difficulties in explaining that it was a balloon.

The pilot also raised questions about whether a regular balloon would be able to withstand the storm conditions.

According to him, the plane had experienced moderate turbulence and ice formation on the engines while passing near clouds.

However, these circumstances do not definitively rule out the possibility of a balloon or other ordinary object. The identity, size, distance, and actual motion of the object have not been independently determined.

NUFORC calls for more serious investigation into reports from pilots

After the case was published, NUFORC raised concerns about how reports of unidentified objects near civilian aircraft are handled.

The organization said there was no evidence that the FAA had referred the case to other agencies for a parallel investigation.

According to NUFORC, objects that appear in controlled airspace should be examined seriously, regardless of whether they turn out to be balloons, drones, or other flying vehicles.

The organization also criticized the reaction of an air traffic controller, who, according to an audio recording, had joked with the pilots for reporting the incident.

"Make sure to include the color of the alien," the controller is heard saying.

NUFORC argues that such reactions could reinforce prejudice against UFO reports and discourage pilots from notifying authorities about unknown objects.

Air safety issue, not proof of extraterrestrials

The organization emphasizes that even if the object turns out to have been a balloon, its presence at high altitudes and near flight corridors could pose a risk.

A potential collision with an aircraft moving at hundreds of kilometers per hour could cause serious injuries.

Furthermore, identifying unknown objects is also important for national security, especially when there is the possibility of using balloons for surveillance.

So far, there is no verified evidence that the object photographed over Ohio is of extraterrestrial origin. The term UFO, or unidentified aerial phenomenon (UAP), only means that the object has not been identified from the available information. The case remains unexplained in the published report, while the testimony of the pilots and the photograph taken require further analysis to determine its nature. /GazetaExpress/
